mainTopic: Settling a contradiction in רבי אלעזר's statements, then the new משנה about hazards placed in רשות הרבים (spilled water, hidden thorns and glass, thorn fences, a fallen wall), and רב's limit on the water case.
overview: The עמוד opens by finishing a question from the previous page: רבי אלעזר ruled one way but quoted his teacher רבי ישמעאל saying the opposite. The answer is simple: one ruling is his own, and the other is his teacher's. A new משנה then makes a person liable for hazards he puts in רשות הרבים, such as spilled water, hidden thorns or glass, a thorn fence, or a fallen wall. רב limits the water case to dirtied clothes, and the גמרא explains why this case and the earlier jug case are both needed: one is about summer and the other about the rainy season. רבי יוחנן limits the thorn case to thorns that stick out into the street, and the גמרא discusses who pays when thorns hidden in someone else's wall fall out, and when a pit is covered with someone else's bucket. Stories of חסידים who got rid of their thorns completely lead to sayings about how to become a חסיד. A second משנה makes a person liable for straw, hay, and dung left in the street. The גמרא asks whether that fits רבי יהודה, who allows fertilizer in the street, and goes back and forth over whether permission frees a person from paying. רב נחמן answers that the משנה is about a time outside fertilizer season, and רב אשי begins another answer that continues on the next עמוד.

steps.title: Finishing the challenge from רבי ישמעאל's teaching
steps.stepSummary: The tail end of a challenge: רבי אלעזר himself quoted רבי ישמעאל with a ruling that seems to contradict רבי אלעזר's own ruling.
steps.simpleTranslation: [But רבי אלעזר said] in the name of רבי ישמעאל, etc.!
steps.whatsHappening: This is the last line of a question that began on the previous עמוד. The גמרא points out that רבי אלעזר quoted רבי ישמעאל saying something that clashes with what רבי אלעזר just ruled.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי אלעזר had ruled that a person is exempt. But he also quoted רבי ישמעאל, who holds a person liable for a בור dug in רשות הרבים, even though it is not his property. The same person seems to be saying two opposite things.

keyTerms.meaning: In the name of. A teaching quoted from someone else.
Short for וכולי, meaning "etc." The rest of the quote is left out because it was already said.

steps.confusionAlert: This line is not a new statement. It is the end of a question that started on the previous עמוד, so read it as part of that challenge.

phrases.english: [He said] in the name of Rabbi Yishmael, etc.!
phrases.notes: The question started on the previous עמוד. The full quote is about someone being liable for a pit in the public area.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Completes a קשיא begun on the previous עמוד.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: רבי אלעזר himself quoted רבי ישמעאל saying a person is liable, so his own ruling seems to contradict his own quote.

steps.title: One ruling is his own, the other is his teacher's
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that רבי אלעזר's exemption is his own opinion, while the liability he quoted belongs to his teacher רבי ישמעאל.
steps.simpleTranslation: It is not difficult. This one is his own view, and that one is his teacher's view.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא resolves the contradiction. It explains that the two rulings come from two different people.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי אלעזר was faithfully reporting what רבי ישמעאל taught, but he does not agree with it himself. So there is no contradiction: a student can quote his teacher and still hold differently.

keyTerms.meaning: It is not difficult. The standard opening of an answer.

steps.whatToRemember: Quoting a teacher is not the same as agreeing with him. רבי אלעזר's own view exempts, while רבי ישמעאל's view makes one liable.

phrases.english: It is not difficult; this is his own [view].
phrases.notes: "This" is רבי אלעזר's ruling that the person is exempt.

phrases.english: That is his teacher's [view].

steps.triggerLanguage: לָא קַשְׁיָא; הָא דִידֵיהּ. הָא דְרַבֵּיהּ.
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the קשיא of step 1.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Attribution split: the two rulings belong to two different people.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Both rulings were thought to be רבי אלעזר's own opinion.
steps.terutzMaskana: The exemption is רבי אלעזר's own view. The liability is רבי ישמעאל's view, which רבי אלעזר quoted but disagrees with.

steps.title: משנה: pouring water in the public area
steps.stepSummary: The משנה rules that someone who pours water into רשות הרבים is liable if another person is damaged by it.
steps.simpleTranslation: משנה: One who pours water in the public domain, and someone else is damaged by it, is liable for his damage.
steps.whatsHappening: A new משנה begins. Its first case is a person who spills water in a public place, where someone else then gets hurt or damaged.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Water left in a public place is a hazard the person created. So the one who poured it must pay for the damage it causes.

keyTerms.meaning: Short for מתניתין, "our משנה." A new משנה starts here.
The public domain, a place everyone uses.
He is liable to pay for his damage.

phrases.english: MISHNA: One who pours water in the public domain,
and another person was damaged by it,
he is liable for his damage.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Begins a new משנה, separate from the previous discussion.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Pouring water in רשות הרבים makes one liable for damage it causes others.

steps.title: משנה: hidden thorns and glass, thorn fences, and a fallen wall
steps.stepSummary: The משנה adds more hazards that make a person liable: hiding a thorn or glass, fencing with thorns, or a wall that fell into the public area.
steps.simpleTranslation: One who hides a thorn or glass, or fences his fence with thorns, or a wall that fell into the public domain, and others were damaged by them, is liable for their damage.
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה continues with three more cases of hazards near the public area. In each case, if people get hurt, the owner pays.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Each case is something sharp or blocking that the person is responsible for and that can hurt passersby. The same rule applies to all of them: he is liable for damage they cause.

keyTerms.meaning: One who hides away or tucks something in.

phrases.english: One who conceals a thorn or glass;
or one who fences his fence with thorns;
or a wall that fell into the public domain;
and others were damaged by them –
he is liable for their damage.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the משנה with more cases that follow the same rule.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Hiding a thorn or glass, fencing with thorns, or a wall falling into רשות הרבים makes one liable for resulting damage.

steps.title: רב: liable only for dirtied clothes, not bodily injury
steps.stepSummary: רב limits the water case: the pourer pays only if the victim's clothes were dirtied. If the victim himself was hurt, the pourer is exempt, because the ground caused the injury.
steps.simpleTranslation: גמרא: רב said: They only taught this when his clothes were soiled by the water. But if he himself was hurt, the pourer is exempt, because the ground of the world injured him.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא begins discussing the משנה. רב narrows the water case to damage to clothing only.
steps.deeperAnalysis: When someone slips on water and gets hurt, the actual blow comes from hitting the ground, not from the water. The ground is not anyone's hazard, so the pourer does not pay for the bodily injury. Dirty water soiling clothes is direct damage from the water, so he pays for that.

keyTerms.meaning: Short for גמרא. The discussion of the משנה starts here.
They only taught [this ruling] when... A formula that limits a ruling.
His clothes or belongings got dirty.
The ground of the world, meaning the natural ground that nobody owns.

steps.confusionAlert: Don't read רב as saying the pourer never pays when someone slips. He pays for the dirtied clothes. Only the injury from hitting the ground is exempt.
steps.whyThisMatters: This sets up the rest of the סוגיא. The גמרא will go on to examine how רב's split between clothing and bodily injury fits with other rules of damages.

phrases.english: GEMARA: Rav said:

phrases.aramaic: לֹא שָׁנוּ אֶלָּא דְּנִטְנְפוּ כֵּלָיו בְּמַיִם,
phrases.english: They taught [this] only where his clothes were soiled by the water,
but [if] he himself [was hurt], [the pourer] is exempt;
the ground of the world injured him.
phrases.notes: He means the man was hurt by hitting the ground when he fell, not by the water itself.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב: לֹא שָׁנוּ אֶלָּא דְּנִטְנְפוּ כֵּלָיו בְּמַיִם
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Opens the גמרא by limiting the משנה's first case (step 3).
steps.mimraCoreRuling: In the water case, the pourer is liable only for soiled clothing. Bodily injury is exempt because the ground caused it.

steps.title: רב הונא: The water should be no better than his own filth
steps.stepSummary: רב הונא challenges רב: even if the water is treated like filth he threw into the street, the pourer should still be liable for the injury.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב הונא said to רב: Let it be no worse than his filth!
steps.whatsHappening: רב הונא pushes back on רב's ruling that the pourer is exempt when the victim is physically hurt. He argues that the water should be treated at least like filth a person throws into the street.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Someone who throws his filth into רשות הרבים is responsible for damage it causes. The water mixed with the dirt makes mud, and that mud comes from the pourer. So why should רב say the ground caused the injury and exempt him?

keyTerms.meaning: 'Let it be no worse than', a way of comparing to a case where the law is clear

phrases.english: Rav Huna said to Rav:
Let it be no worse than his filth!
phrases.notes: He means: even if you only count the water as the man's own mud or filth in the street, he should still have to pay.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַר לֵיהּ רַב הוּנָא לְרַב לֹא יְהֵא אֶלָּא כְּרִפְשׁוֹ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Directly challenges רב's exemption from step 5.
steps.kashyaTarget: רב's ruling that the pourer is exempt when the victim himself is injured
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A person is liable for filth he throws into the street; the mud made by his water should be no better, so he should be liable.

steps.title: רב: I am talking about water that already soaked in
steps.stepSummary: רב answers that his exemption is for a case where the water was already absorbed into the ground, so there is no mud left that belongs to the pourer.
steps.simpleTranslation: Do you think this is where the water did not soak in? It is where the water soaked in.
steps.whatsHappening: רב answers רב הונא by explaining exactly which case he meant. He is talking about water that has already soaked into the ground.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the water is still sitting there as mud, רב הונא would be right that it is like the pourer's filth. But once the water has soaked in, nothing of the pourer's is left; there is only damp ground. So the ground itself caused the fall, and the pourer is exempt.

keyTerms.meaning: 'Do you think...?', used to correct a mistaken assumption
The water was used up, meaning it soaked into the ground

steps.whatToRemember: רב's exemption is only for water that has already soaked in. If the mud from the water is still there, it is like the pourer's own filth.

phrases.english: Do you think it is where the water did not soak in?!
It is where the water soaked in.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers רב הונא's challenge in step 6 by narrowing the case.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: רב הונא assumed the water was still sitting there as mud, like the pourer's filth.
steps.terutzMaskana: רב means the water already soaked in, so only the ground is there and the pourer is exempt for bodily injury.

steps.title: Why do we need two משניות for the same law?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks: if the water case is only about dirtied clothes, why do we need it, since the earlier משנה already taught the same law?
steps.simpleTranslation: And why do I need two?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks why there are two משניות that seem to teach the same thing. According to רב, both are about clothes getting dirty from spilled water.
steps.deeperAnalysis: An earlier משנה taught about a jug that broke and spilled water, dirtying a passerby's clothes. If our משנה is also only about dirtied clothes, as רב says, it seems to add nothing new.

keyTerms.meaning: 'Why do I need two?', asking why the same law is taught twice

phrases.english: And why do I need two?
phrases.notes: The 'two' are our משנה about pouring water and the earlier משנה about a jug that broke and spilled water, which also dirtied someone's clothes.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: After רב's reading is settled, the גמרא points out that this reading seems to make the משנה repeat itself.
steps.kashyaTarget: רב's reading of the משנה as being only about dirtied clothes
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If both משניות teach liability for dirtied clothes from spilled water, one of them is extra.

steps.title: One case is in summer and one is in the rainy season
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that the two משניות are not the same: one is about summer and the other is about the rainy season.
steps.simpleTranslation: One is in the summer, and one is in the rainy season.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the question of why we need two משניות. Each one is about a different time of year.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The two משניות are not saying the exact same thing, because one is about summer and the other is about the rainy season. Since the season changes the situation, each case teaches something of its own, and neither is extra.
steps.whatToRemember: According to רב, the water משנה is about dirtied clothes. It is not a repeat of the jug משנה, because one משנה is about summer and the other is about the rainy season.

phrases.english: One is in the summer,
and one is in the rainy season.

steps.triggerLanguage: חֲדָא בִּימוֹת הַחַמָּה וַחֲדָא בִּימוֹת הַגְּשָׁמִים
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question about the two משניות in step 8.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Splitting the cases (each source covers a different situation)
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The two משניות seemed to repeat the same law about dirtied clothes.
steps.terutzMaskana: One משנה is about summer and the other is about the rainy season, so both are needed.

steps.title: A ברייתא shows the difference between summer and the rainy season
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא teaches that pouring waste water into the street is forbidden in summer and allowed in the rainy season, but you still pay if it causes damage.
steps.simpleTranslation: As a ברייתא teaches: all those people the Sages spoke about, who open their gutters into the street and flush out their caves into the street, are not allowed to do so in summer, but are allowed to in the rainy season. And even though they did it with permission, if it caused damage, they must pay.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a ברייתא to support its last answer, that one משנה is about summer and the other is about the rainy season.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא proves that the season really does change the law: in summer you may not pour, while in the rainy season you may. It also proves that even when pouring is allowed, you still pay for damage. That is why both משניות are needed, one for each season.

keyTerms.meaning: Open their gutters (to drain waste into the street)

steps.whatToRemember: Having permission to do something does not free you from paying if it causes damage.
steps.whyThisMatters: This sets a big principle in נזיקין: doing something you are allowed to do does not by itself remove your responsibility for the harm it causes.

phrases.english: As it was taught: all those whom they said
phrases.notes: "Whom they said" means the people the Sages allowed to do these things.

phrases.english: may open their gutters
and flush out their caves
phrases.notes: These are pits where smelly water was kept; they empty them out into the street.

phrases.english: in the summer they do not have permission,
and in the rainy season they have permission.
And even though it is with permission,
if they caused damage, they are liable to pay.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Supports the answer in step 9 that the two משניות refer to different seasons.
steps.raayaObject: The answer in step 9 that one משנה is about summer and the other about the rainy season.
steps.raayaSupportSource: A ברייתא that permits pouring in the rainy season but not summer, and requires payment for damage either way.

steps.title: רבי יוחנן limits the hidden thorn ruling to thorns sticking out
steps.stepSummary: On the משנה about hiding a thorn, רבי יוחנן says the person is liable only if the thorns stick out into the street, not if they stay inside his own space.
steps.simpleTranslation: The משנה said: one who hides a thorn, etc. רבי יוחנן said: they only taught this when he lets it stick out into the street, but if he keeps it within his own area, he is not liable.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא moves to a new line of the משנה, about hiding a thorn or glass or making a thorn fence. רבי יוחנן narrows when the person is liable.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה made the person liable for damage from thorns. רבי יוחנן says that is only when the thorns poke out into the public street. If they stay inside his own property line, he is exempt.

keyTerms.meaning: One who hides or tucks something away
They only taught this in the case of
Lets it stick out (into the street)
Keeps it tightly inside his own area

phrases.english: One who hides a thorn, etc.
Rabbi Yochanan said:
They only taught this when he lets it stick out,
phrases.notes: Literally "makes it fly": the thorns jut out past his wall into the street.

phrases.english: but if he keeps it inside, no.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new topic from the next line of the משנה.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The person who hides thorns is liable only if they stick out into the street; if they stay within his own area, he is exempt.

steps.title: Why is he exempt when the thorns stay inside?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks for the reason he is exempt in the case where the thorns stay within his own area.
steps.simpleTranslation: What is the reason he is exempt?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks why רבי יוחנן exempts the person whose thorns don't stick out. This sets up the answer in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Someone could still get hurt by those thorns, so why shouldn't he pay? The גמרא wants the logic behind the exemption.

keyTerms.meaning: Exempt, does not have to pay

phrases.english: What is the reason he is exempt?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks for the reason behind רבי יוחנן's exemption.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Why is the person exempt when the thorns stay within his own space?

steps.title: People don't usually rub against walls
steps.stepSummary: רב אחא בריה דרב איקא explains that people normally don't brush up against walls, so getting hurt by thorns inside the wall line is unusual.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב אחא בריה דרב איקא said: because people don't normally rub up against walls.
steps.whatsHappening: רב אחא בריה דרב איקא answers the question of why the person is exempt.
steps.deeperAnalysis: People walking in the street normally keep a little distance from walls. So if thorns stay inside the wall line, someone who gets hurt by them did something unusual, and the owner is not to blame. Thorns sticking out into the walkway are different, because people walk there normally.

keyTerms.meaning: To rub or brush up against

steps.whatToRemember: Thorns that stick out into the street make you liable; thorns kept inside your wall line do not, because people don't normally rub against walls.

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר רַב אַחָא בְּרֵיהּ דְּרַב אִיקָא:
phrases.english: Rav Acha, son of Rav Ika, said:

phrases.aramaic: לְפִי שֶׁאֵין דַּרְכָּן שֶׁל בְּנֵי אָדָם
phrases.english: Because it is not the way of people
to rub against walls.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב אַחָא בְּרֵיהּ דְּרַב אִיקָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 12.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: People don't normally brush against walls, so an injury from thorns inside the wall line is unusual, and the owner is exempt.

steps.title: Thorns hidden in a friend's wall that he knocked down
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא rules that if someone hid thorns or glass in another person's wall, and the owner knocked down the wall so it fell into the street and caused damage, the one who hid them pays.
steps.simpleTranslation: The Rabbis taught: if someone hides his thorns and glass inside another person's wall, and the wall's owner comes and knocks down his wall, and it falls into the street, and they cause damage, the one who hid them is liable.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a ברייתא with a new case about thorns hidden in someone else's wall.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Here two people are involved: the one who hid the thorns, and the wall owner who knocked down the wall. The ברייתא puts the blame on the one who hid them, even though the owner's action is what sent them into the street.

phrases.english: The Rabbis taught:
One who hides his thorns and his pieces of glass
inside another person's wall,
and the owner of the wall came and knocked down his wall,
and it fell into the public street,
and they caused damage, the one who hid them is liable.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Brings a related ברייתא about hidden thorns, now inside someone else's wall.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: If the wall owner knocks down a wall with hidden thorns and they fall into the street and cause damage, the one who hid them is liable.

steps.title: רבי יוחנן limits the ברייתא to a shaky wall
steps.stepSummary: רבי יוחנן says the hider pays only if the wall was shaky; if the wall was strong, the hider is exempt and the wall owner pays.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי יוחנן said: they only taught this about a shaky wall. But with a strong wall, the one who hid them is exempt, and the owner of the wall is liable.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי יוחנן narrows the ברייתא, explaining when the hider pays and when the wall owner pays instead.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the wall was shaky, the hider should have expected it to be torn down soon, so he is to blame. If the wall was strong, the hider had no reason to expect that, so the owner who knocked it down is responsible. The blame moves depending on the wall's condition.
steps.whatToRemember: With a shaky wall, the hider pays; with a strong wall, the wall owner who knocked it down pays.
steps.confusionAlert: Don't think the ברייתא always blames the hider. רבי יוחנן says that is only for a shaky wall; with a strong wall, the blame flips to the wall owner.

phrases.english: Rabbi Yochanan said:
They only taught this about a shaky wall,
but with a strong wall,
the one who hid them is exempt, and the owner of the wall is liable.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן: לֹא שָׁנוּ אֶלָּא בְּכוֹתֶל רָעוּעַ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Limits the ruling of the ברייתא in step 14 to a shaky wall.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The hider is liable only when the wall was shaky; with a strong wall, the hider is exempt and the wall owner is liable.

steps.title: רבינא's lesson: covering a pit with someone else's bucket
steps.stepSummary: רבינא learns from רבי יוחנן's ruling that if a person covers his בור with a friend's bucket, and the friend takes his bucket back, the owner of the בור is liable for any damage.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבינא said: This teaches that if someone covers his pit with his friend's bucket, and the bucket's owner comes and takes his bucket, the owner of the pit is liable.
steps.whatsHappening: רבינא draws a new rule from רבי יוחנן's shaky-wall ruling in Step 15 and applies it to a pit covered with a borrowed bucket.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In the shaky-wall case, the person who hid the thorns pays, because the cover was never going to last. A bucket that belongs to someone else is the same kind of cover, because its owner can take it back any time. So the בור owner never really covered his pit, and he is the one who pays.

keyTerms.meaning: This teaches us / this shows that (a rule drawn from an earlier ruling)
The owner of the pit, the one responsible for it

steps.whyThisMatters: It shows that a weak or temporary cover does not free a person from responsibility for his own hazard.

phrases.english: Ravina said: This teaches us
phrases.notes: He is drawing a lesson from רבי יוחנן's shaky-wall ruling (Step 15).

phrases.english: one who covers his pit with his friend's bucket,
and the owner of the bucket came and took his bucket,
the owner of the pit is liable.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Applies רבי יוחנן's shaky-wall distinction to a similar case of a cover that can be removed.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: If a pit is covered with someone else's bucket and the bucket's owner takes it back, the pit owner is liable for damage.

steps.title: Isn't this obvious?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges רבינא: his rule seems to be exactly רבי יוחנן's shaky-wall ruling, so what is new?
steps.simpleTranslation: Obvious!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא objects that רבינא's statement adds nothing, because it looks the same as רבי יוחנן's ruling.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A borrowed bucket is just like a shaky wall: in both cases the cover was likely to be removed from the start. If the rules match, why does רבינא need to say it at all?

keyTerms.meaning: It's obvious! (a challenge that a statement teaches nothing new)

phrases.english: That's obvious!
phrases.notes: Obvious from רבי יוחנן's shaky-wall ruling: the cover was always going to come off.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges רבינא's statement in Step 16 as adding nothing new.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The bucket case matches the shaky-wall case exactly, so stating it separately seems pointless.

steps.title: The new point: the bucket owner does not have to warn the pit owner
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that we might have thought the bucket owner must warn the בור owner, because he knows who he is. רבינא teaches that he does not have to.
steps.simpleTranslation: You might have said: Only there, in the wall case, is the wall owner exempt, because he did not know who hid the thorns so he could tell him. But here, where the bucket owner knows the pit owner, he should have told him. So רבינא teaches us that he does not have to.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains what is new in רבינא's statement by pointing to a real difference between the two cases.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In the wall case, the wall owner has no idea who hid the thorns, so he could not warn anyone. In the bucket case, the bucket owner knows exactly whose pit it is, so we might expect him to give a warning before taking his bucket. רבינא teaches that he still has no such duty, and the בור owner alone is liable.

keyTerms.meaning: You might have said (introduces the mistaken thought being corrected)
To inform him / let him know

steps.confusionAlert: The "he should have informed him" line is the mistaken idea. The conclusion is that the bucket owner does NOT have to warn anyone.
steps.whatToRemember: Someone who takes back his own property that was covering another person's pit does not have to warn the pit owner. The pit owner stays fully liable.

phrases.english: You might have said:

phrases.aramaic: הָתָם הוּא דְּלָא הֲוִי יָדַע לֵיהּ –
phrases.english: Only there, because he did not know him
phrases.notes: "There" is the thorns-in-the-wall case, where the wall owner did not know who hid the thorns.

phrases.english: so that he could inform him;
but here, where he does know him,
he should have informed him;
so it teaches us otherwise.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the פשיטא challenge by showing a difference between the two cases.
steps.terutzResolutionType: מהו דתימא: identifies a reasonable mistaken assumption that the statement rules out
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Because the bucket owner knows the pit owner, he should have to warn him before taking his bucket, and he would share the blame if he did not.
steps.terutzMaskana: The bucket owner has no duty to warn. The pit owner is liable.

steps.title: How the early pious people buried their thorns and glass
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא relates that the חסידים הראשונים hid thorns and glass in their own fields, buried three טפחים deep so even a plow would not reach them.
steps.simpleTranslation: The Sages taught: The early pious people would hide their thorns and glass inside their own fields, and would dig three handbreadths deep for them, so that the plow would not be stopped by them.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a ברייתא showing the ideal way to get rid of dangerous items, going beyond what the law requires.
steps.deeperAnalysis: So far we learned when someone who hides thorns is liable. The חסידים הראשונים were extra careful: they buried their hazards in their own land and deep enough that plowing would not dig them back up. That way, no one could ever be hurt.

keyTerms.meaning: The early pious people, who acted beyond the letter of the law

steps.whyThisMatters: It sets a model of extra care with hazards: get rid of them so completely that they can never cause harm.

phrases.english: The Sages taught:
The early pious people
would hide their thorns and their pieces of glass
inside their own fields,
and would dig three handbreadths deep for them
so that the plow would not be stopped by them.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves from liability for hidden hazards to the pious ideal of disposing of them safely.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The חסידים הראשונים buried thorns and glass in their own fields, three טפחים deep, so they could never cause harm or catch on a plow.

steps.title: רב ששת and רבא destroyed their thorns completely
steps.stepSummary: רב ששת burned his thorns and glass, and רבא threw them into the Tigris River, so they could never hurt anyone.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב ששת would throw them into the fire. רבא would throw them into the Tigris River.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא keeps telling how great people made sure their sharp objects could never hurt anyone. רב ששת burned them and רבא threw them into the river.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The חסידים הראשונים buried thorns and glass three טפחים deep in their own fields. רב ששת and רבא went one step further and got rid of them completely. Burned or swept away by the river, these things could never hurt anyone at all.

phrases.english: Rav Sheshet would throw them into the fire.
phrases.notes: "Them" means the thorns and glass from the story of the חסידים הראשונים just before this.

phrases.english: Rava would throw them into the Tigris River.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds later אמוראים whose practice went even further than the חסידים הראשונים in Step 19.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Truly careful people destroy dangerous objects so they can never cause damage.

steps.title: רב יהודה: a would-be pious person should keep the laws of damages
steps.stepSummary: רב יהודה says that someone who wants to be a חסיד should carefully keep the laws of נזיקין.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב יהודה said: whoever wants to be a חסיד should fulfill the matters of נזיקין.
steps.whatsHappening: Building on the stories of careful חסידים, רב יהודה says that the path to being a חסיד runs through the laws of damages.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The stories above showed great people going beyond the letter of the law so they would not harm others. רב יהודה turns this into a general rule. Real piety starts with being very careful never to damage another person or his property.

keyTerms.meaning: a pious person who goes beyond what the law requires

phrases.english: Rav Yehuda said:
One who wants to be pious
should fulfill the matters of נזיקין.
phrases.notes: He means the laws about damages, the same area of law this whole מסכתא deals with.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Turns the חסידים stories into a general rule about how to become pious.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Piety begins with carefully keeping the laws of damages.

steps.title: רבא: the matters of אבות, or of ברכות
steps.stepSummary: רבא names a different area: the matters of אבות. A second version of his statement says the matters of ברכות.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא said: the matters of אבות. Some say: the matters of ברכות.
steps.whatsHappening: רבא gives his own answer to the question of how to become a חסיד. The גמרא also records a second version of what he said.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב יהודה pointed to piety between a person and his friend, which means not causing damage. רבא points to the matters of אבות, which teach good character and ethics. In the other version he points to the matters of ברכות, the blessings we say to thank and praise ה׳.

keyTerms.meaning: the matters of מסכת אבות (ethics and good character)

steps.whatToRemember: Three ways to become a חסיד: be careful with damages (רב יהודה), live by the ethics of אבות (רבא), or be careful with ברכות (the other version of רבא).

phrases.english: Rava said: the matters of Avot.
And some say: the matters of Berachot.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives a different answer to רב יהודה's statement about the path to piety.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The path to piety is the matters of אבות, or in the other version, the matters of ברכות.

steps.title: משנה: straw and hay left in the public domain
steps.stepSummary: A person who puts his straw and hay in רשות הרבים to turn into fertilizer must pay if they hurt someone, and anyone who takes them first gets to keep them.
steps.simpleTranslation: משנה: A person took his straw and hay out to רשות הרבים so they would become fertilizer, and someone was hurt by them. He must pay for the damage, and whoever takes the straw and hay first gets to keep them.
steps.whatsHappening: A new משנה begins here. It deals with a person who leaves straw and hay in the street so they will rot into fertilizer.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The owner has a practical reason to put them there, but they block the public road. So he must pay if anyone gets hurt. The משנה also says he can lose them: whoever grabs them first may keep them.

keyTerms.meaning: straw and hay (stalks left over from grain)
whoever takes them first acquires them

phrases.english: Mishnah:
One who takes out his straw and his hay
to the public domain to become fertilizer,
and another person was harmed by them,
he is liable for his damage,
and whoever takes them first acquires them.

steps.triggerLanguage: הַמּוֹצִיא אֶת תִּבְנוֹ וְקַשּׁוֹ לִרְשׁוּת הָרַבִּים לִזְבָלִים
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new משנה. It continues the theme of objects left where they can hurt the public.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A person who leaves straw and hay in רשות הרבים pays for any damage they cause, and anyone who takes them first may keep them.

steps.title: רבן שמעון בן גמליאל: every public obstacle follows this rule
steps.stepSummary: רבן שמעון בן גמליאל says that anyone who creates any obstacle in רשות הרבים pays for the damage it causes, and anyone who takes it first gets to keep it.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבן שמעון בן גמליאל says: all who spoil רשות הרבים with obstacles that cause damage must pay, and whoever takes those things first gets to keep them.
steps.whatsHappening: רבן שמעון בן גמליאל takes the rule about straw and hay and widens it to every kind of obstacle placed in public.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The first part of the משנה spoke only about straw and hay. רבן שמעון בן גמליאל applies both parts of the rule to anything that spoils the public road. The person must pay for damage, and others may take the object.

keyTerms.meaning: those who spoil, here meaning people who put obstacles in public

phrases.english: Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel says:
all who place obstacles in the public domain, and they caused damage,
are liable to pay,
and whoever takes them first acquires them.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Expands the straw-and-hay rule from Step 23 to every kind of public obstacle.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Anyone who creates an obstacle in רשות הרבים pays for the damage it causes, and others may take the obstacle.

steps.title: Turning over dung in the public domain
steps.stepSummary: A person who turns over dung in רשות הרבים is liable if someone is hurt by it.
steps.simpleTranslation: If a person turns over dung in רשות הרבים and someone is hurt by it, he must pay for the damage.
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה adds one more case: a person who did not put the dung there but turned it over.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Here the person did not bring the dung into the street. He only moved or turned it over. Still, the משנה makes him liable for the damage it causes.
steps.whatToRemember: The משנה makes three points. Straw and hay left in public make the owner liable, and anyone may take them. רבן שמעון בן גמליאל applies this to all obstacles. Even someone who only turns over dung in public is liable.

phrases.english: One who turns over dung in the public domain,
and another person was harmed by it,
he is liable for his damage.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds a further case to the משנה's rules about obstacles in רשות הרבים.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A person who turns over dung in רשות הרבים is liable for any damage it causes.

steps.title: Does the משנה disagree with רבי יהודה?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא suggests that the משנה's ruling, that one pays for damage from straw in the street, does not match the view of רבי יהודה.
steps.simpleTranslation: גמרא: Shall we say that our משנה does not follow רבי יהודה?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא opens its discussion of the משנה by proposing that it goes against the view of רבי יהודה. This line sets up the next step, where the גמרא shows the source for רבי יהודה's view.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה (step 23) said that whoever puts straw and hay in רשות הרבים must pay if it causes damage. The גמרא suspects that a תנא who allows people to put such things in the street would not make them pay. The proof comes in the next step.

keyTerms.meaning: The discussion that analyzes the משנה
Shall we say. Introduces a suggestion the גמרא wants to test

phrases.english: GEMARA: Shall we say that our משנה
is not in accordance with רבי יהודה?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Begins the גמרא's analysis of the משנה quoted in step 23
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Whether the משנה's rule that one pays for damage from straw in the street contradicts רבי יהודה

steps.title: רבי יהודה allows fertilizer in the street for thirty days
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא quotes רבי יהודה: during fertilizer season, a person may pile his fertilizer in רשות הרבים for thirty days, since יהושע divided the land on that condition.
steps.simpleTranslation: As a ברייתא teaches: רבי יהודה says, during the season when fertilizer is taken out, a person may take his fertilizer out to the street and pile it there for thirty days, so that people and animals trample it. יהושע gave out the land on that condition.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings the source behind its suggestion. רבי יהודה says putting fertilizer in the street is allowed, built right into the terms on which יהושע divided ארץ ישראל.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If putting fertilizer in the street is fully permitted, it seems the owner should not have to pay for damage it causes. That would contradict the משנה, which makes him pay. So the משנה seems not to follow רבי יהודה.

keyTerms.meaning: Taking out fertilizer, the season when it is put out
Gave as an inheritance, divided the land

phrases.english: As it is taught in a ברייתא: רבי יהודה says:
At the time when fertilizer is taken out,
a person may take his fertilizer out to the public domain
and pile it up there for a full thirty days,
so that it gets trampled
by people's feet and by animals' feet.
For it was on this condition
that יהושע gave out the land.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Supplies the source for the suggestion in step 26
steps.raayaObject: That רבי יהודה would not make one pay for damage from things put in the street, unlike the משנה
steps.raayaSupportSource: A ברייתא where רבי יהודה permits piling fertilizer in רשות הרבים for thirty days

steps.title: רבי יהודה may agree that one pays for damage
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא rejects the suggestion: even רבי יהודה may agree that if the fertilizer causes damage, its owner pays.
steps.simpleTranslation: You can even say the משנה follows רבי יהודה. רבי יהודה agrees that if it caused damage, he pays for the damage it caused.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes back and says the משנה can match רבי יהודה after all.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Being allowed to put fertilizer in the street is one thing. Paying for damage it causes is another. רבי יהודה only gave permission to put it there; he never said the owner is free from paying. So there is no contradiction with the משנה.
steps.confusionAlert: Do not mix up "allowed to do it" with "free from paying." Here the גמרא separates the two: permission to put it there, but still liable for damage.

phrases.english: You can even say it follows רבי יהודה,
for רבי יהודה agrees
that if it caused damage,
he pays for the damage it caused.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the suggestion of steps 26 and 27
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: Rejects the claim that the משנה disagrees with רבי יהודה
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: The suggestion assumed that permission to put fertilizer in the street means no payment for damage, but permission and liability can be separate

steps.title: רבי יהודה exempts a נר חנוכה because it had permission
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges: in a משנה, רבי יהודה exempts the owner of a נר חנוכה from damage because it was placed with permission, apparently permission of the court.
steps.simpleTranslation: But we learned in a משנה: רבי יהודה says, with a נר חנוכה he is exempt, because it was there with permission. Isn't that because it had the permission of the court?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא attacks the answer of step 28 using another ruling of רבי יהודה. There, permission does seem to free a person from paying.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 28 said that for רבי יהודה, permission does not remove the duty to pay. But in the נר חנוכה case, רבי יהודה exempts the owner just because he had permission. If court permission exempts there, it should exempt here too, since the fertilizer was also put out with permission.

keyTerms.meaning: What, is it not...? Proposes the likely reading of a source

phrases.english: But didn't we learn in a משנה: רבי יהודה says:
With a Chanukah lamp, he is exempt,
phrases.notes: This is the משנה on 62b about a lamp outside a store that sets fire to something passing in the street.

phrases.english: because it was there with permission.

phrases.aramaic: מַאי, לָאו מִשּׁוּם רְשׁוּת בֵּית דִּין?
phrases.english: What, is it not because of the permission of the court?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the answer given in step 28
steps.kashyaTarget: The claim in step 28 that רבי יהודה makes a person pay for damage even when he acted with permission
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: רבי יהודה exempts the Chanukah lamp owner because of court permission. So permission should also exempt the person who put fertilizer in the street, and the משנה, which makes him pay, would not follow רבי יהודה.

steps.title: The נר חנוכה is exempt because it is a מצוה
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that רבי יהודה exempts the owner of the נר חנוכה because of permission for a מצוה, not just the court's permission.
steps.simpleTranslation: No, the reason is the permission given for a מצוה. As a ברייתא teaches: רבי יהודה says that with a נר חנוכה he is exempt, because it is permission for a מצוה.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the challenge from the נר חנוכה. רבי יהודה exempts there only because the lamp was placed outside for a מצוה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The challenge said רבי יהודה exempts anyone who acts with the court's permission. The answer narrows it: only רשות מצוה exempts. Ordinary permission, like piling fertilizer, does not, so the fertilizer owner can still pay, and the משנה can still fit רבי יהודה. A ברייתא quoting רבי יהודה's own reason backs this up.

keyTerms.meaning: Permission granted for doing a מצוה

steps.confusionAlert: The גמרא does not say רבי יהודה ignores the court's permission completely. It says that court permission alone is not enough to exempt you from paying; the extra element of a מצוה is what exempts.

phrases.english: No, it is because of permission for a מצוה.
As it is taught in a baraita: Rabbi Yehuda says:
With a Chanukah lamp, he is exempt,
because it is permission for a מצוה.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the נר חנוכה challenge of step 29, protecting the rejection in step 28.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Distinction: permission for a מצוה versus plain court permission.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: רבי יהודה exempts anyone who acts with the court's permission, including the fertilizer owner.
steps.terutzMaskana: Only permission for a מצוה exempts; the fertilizer owner, who had only plain permission, still pays.

steps.title: A ברייתא shows רבי יהודה exempts anyone allowed to block the street
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא says that רבי יהודה exempts all those permitted to obstruct רשות הרבים, so plain permission does exempt him.
steps.simpleTranslation: Come and hear: All those cases where the חכמים said a person may obstruct רשות הרבים, if they caused damage they must pay, and רבי יהודה exempts them!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a new ברייתא to challenge again. It shows רבי יהודה exempts people who block the street with permission, even without a מצוה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 30 said only a מצוה exempts. But this ברייתא talks about all cases of permission to obstruct the street, like the fertilizer case, and רבי יהודה exempts all of them. So it seems that for רבי יהודה plain permission is enough, and our משנה, which makes the owner pay, does not fit him.

keyTerms.meaning: To obstruct or cause a hazard

phrases.english: Come and hear:
All these cases where the Sages said
that people are permitted to place obstacles in the public domain,
if they caused damage, they are liable to pay;
and Rabbi Yehuda exempts them!

steps.triggerLanguage: תָּא שְׁמַע: כׇּל אֵלּוּ שֶׁאָמְרוּ מוּתָּרִין לְקַלְקֵל בִּרְשׁוּת הָרַבִּים
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the claim that only permission for a מצוה exempts, reviving the suggestion of step 26.
steps.kashyaTarget: The claim (steps 28 and 30) that רבי יהודה would make the fertilizer owner pay.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The ברייתא shows רבי יהודה exempts everyone permitted to obstruct the street, so plain permission exempts, and the משנה's ruling to pay conflicts with him.

steps.title: רב נחמן: the משנה is outside fertilizer season
steps.stepSummary: רב נחמן explains that the משנה is talking about a time that is not fertilizer season, so there was no permission, and it fits רבי יהודה.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב נחמן said: Our משנה is talking about a time that is not the season for taking out fertilizer, and it follows רבי יהודה.
steps.whatsHappening: רב נחמן accepts that רבי יהודה exempts when there is permission. He answers that the משנה is talking about a case with no permission.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי יהודה allows fertilizer in the street only during fertilizer season. If the משנה is talking about other times of the year, the person had no permission at all, so even רבי יהודה makes him pay. So the משנה agrees with רבי יהודה after all.

keyTerms.meaning: The season for taking fertilizer out to the fields

steps.whatToRemember: According to רב נחמן, רבי יהודה exempts someone who left things in the street with permission, and our משנה makes the owner pay only because it is talking about a time when there was no permission.

phrases.english: Rav Nachman said:
Our mishna is not during the time when fertilizer is taken out,
and it follows Rabbi Yehuda.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב נַחְמָן: מַתְנִיתִין – שֶׁלֹּא בִּשְׁעַת הוֹצָאַת זְבָלִים
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers step 31 by limiting the משנה's case to a time without permission.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Limiting the case (אוקימתא): the משנה is outside fertilizer season.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The משנה makes the owner pay even when he had permission, which goes against רבי יהודה.
steps.terutzMaskana: The משנה is about a time with no permission, so it agrees with רבי יהודה.

steps.title: רב אשי begins a different answer
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא introduces רב אשי, who will give another way to fit the משנה with רבי יהודה.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב אשי said:
steps.whatsHappening: This line is a setup. The גמרא is introducing רב אשי, whose answer comes right after this.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב נחמן just gave one way to make the משנה fit רבי יהודה. רב אשי will offer a different explanation. His actual words continue on the next עמוד.

phrases.english: Rav Ashi said:

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Opens an alternative answer to the challenge of step 31, beside רב נחמן's answer.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Alternative answer (content follows in the continuation).
